_about: Explanations written for this website, not part of the paper. 'match' lists the exact spellings to underline in the text (case-sensitive, whole words).

terms.def: A way of solving problems by declaring what a good answer must satisfy (the constraints) rather than how to compute it. A general-purpose solver then searches for values that satisfy every constraint.
A set of variables, the values each variable may take (its domain), and constraints between them. A solution assigns a value to every variable so that all constraints hold.
A CSP whose constraints may be satisfied partly or with a penalty, instead of strictly true/false. Useful when not every wish can be met at once.
A CSP with an objective function added: among all solutions that satisfy the constraints, find the best one.
The classic family of optimization models (linear, quadratic, mixed-integer programs) built on algebra. Very efficient, but the model must fit a strict mathematical form.
An MP model in which the objective and constraints are linear and some variables must be whole numbers.
Using a simulator as a stand-in for the real system, and an optimizer to search for the simulator inputs that give the best outcome.
The person or organization choosing what to do, for example a manager deciding on a buying strategy.
Making structured models of how an organization works: its processes, actors, goals and information.
Learn how controllable inputs affect outcomes from data (here: simulation runs), then put that learned model inside an optimization model so the solver can reason with it.
A function made of layers of simple units. Each unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through an activation function. Here it learns to imitate the simulator.
A model of a model. Here: a fast neural network that approximates a slow simulation model.
The non-linear function applied to each unit's weighted sum. Its shape decides what the network can represent and how hard the network is for a solver to reason about.
The S-shaped activation 1/(1+e^(−x)), squashing any input into (0, 1). Accurate, but the exponential makes it hard for most solvers.
The paper's quadratic alternative 1/(1+x²). It drops the exponential, so solvers such as Gurobi can handle it.
The paper's semi-linear alternative 1/(1+max(0,x)), from the first Taylor term of the sigmoid. Fastest to solve in the experiments.
A function is injective when different inputs always give different outputs, so each output tells you exactly which input produced it.
Optimization where the problem has a single valley (no misleading local optima), so solvers can find the best answer quickly and reliably.
A deterministic sequence of points designed to fill a space evenly, with fewer clumps and gaps than random points.
Monte Carlo methods that use low-discrepancy points instead of random ones, usually giving better estimates with fewer samples.
A low-discrepancy sequence. Each coordinate writes the index in a different prime base (2, 3, 5, …) and mirrors its digits around the decimal point.
A low-discrepancy sequence built from binary 'direction numbers' with bitwise XOR. Very even coverage, especially in low dimensions.
The paper's way to generate objective weights that sum to one: take d−1 low-discrepancy coordinates, keep the point only if they sum to at most 1, and set the last coordinate to 1 minus that sum.
A number measuring how unevenly points cover the unit cube. Lower means more even.
With several objectives, the set of solutions that cannot improve one objective without making another worse. A decision maker picks a trade-off from this set.
A solution that no other solution beats on every objective at once. Together they form the (approximate) Pareto front.
Combining several objectives into one score by a weighted sum. Changing the weights steers the solver toward different trade-offs.
A soft constraint with a weight (how much it matters) and a threshold (when it counts as satisfied).
A soft CSP where each constraint is satisfied to a degree, used in the authors' earlier work with weights and thresholds per objective.
Multi-objective methods that first compute many good trade-offs and only afterwards ask the decision maker which they prefer.
Ready-made constraints that capture a common pattern over many variables at once (such as 'all different'), which solvers handle efficiently.
Encoding each unit of a trained network as a constraint: its value equals the activation of the weighted sum of the previous layer. Appendix B shows real ones.
A value the solver is free to choose, such as how much of each ingredient to buy.
The quantity to maximize or minimize, such as successful orders minus spoilage.
Optimizing a system you can only query (run with inputs, observe outputs) without knowing its inner structure.
Optimization inspired by natural selection: keep a population of candidate inputs, mutate and recombine the best ones, repeat.
Learning the constraints of a model automatically, for example by asking an oracle such as a simulator whether candidate assignments are valid.
The classic trade-off: the more detail a model can express, the harder it usually is to compute with.
The average squared difference between the network's predictions and the simulator's true outputs on test data. Lower is more accurate.
How many Pareto-optimal solutions a method found. More is better (more choice).
The largest distance between any two solutions found. Larger means more diverse trade-offs.
A solver-independent modelling language for constraint problems. One model can be run with many different solvers.
A commercial, state-of-the-art solver for mathematical programming problems.
An open-source Java constraint solver. Slower here, but it supports the sigmoid's exponential.
Google's open-source optimization toolkit, including a constraint programming solver.
A programmable environment for agent-based simulations, where many simple agents interact on a grid.
Design and Engineering Methodology for Organizations: an enterprise modelling method describing an organization through its transactions.
A simulation made of many individual actors following simple rules. Interesting behaviour emerges from their interactions.
The discipline of modelling, analysing and improving an organization's workflows.
Decidables are inputs you control (e.g. how much to buy); observables are quantities you can only measure (e.g. spoilage).
The activation max(0, x). Appendix B's hidden layers use it, written as max((…), 0).
